name: SpaceX Raptor 2
source: SpaceX public statements (2022), compiled in Wikipedia 'SpaceX Raptor'. Vacuum thrust derived from mass flow at the quoted Isp.
notes: Best public estimate; Raptor specs change often and are not formally published.

name: SpaceX Raptor Vacuum
source: SpaceX public statements, compiled in Wikipedia 'SpaceX Raptor'. Sea-level figures derived from a 2.3 m nozzle exit and are not a real rating.
notes: Best public estimate. Vacuum nozzle: not designed to fire at sea level.

name: Blue Origin BE-4
source: Blue Origin (2,400 kN sea-level thrust). Isp and mass are third-party estimates (Wikipedia 'BE-4').
notes: Best public estimate; Isp and mass are not published by Blue Origin.

name: Rocketdyne F-1
source: NASA Saturn V Flight Manual SA-503 (MSFC-MAN-503); Rocketdyne F-1 data sheet.

name: Rocketdyne J-2
source: NASA Saturn V Flight Manual SA-503 (MSFC-MAN-503); Rocketdyne J-2 data sheet.

name: Service module engine (methalox)
source: Free-design estimate: Apollo SPS thrust class (91 kN) with a methalox vacuum Isp.
notes: No real small methalox engine in the catalog fits a 4 m service module, so this one is estimated.

name: SLS five-segment booster
source: NASA SLS Solid Rocket Booster fact sheet (FS-2020-08); thrust-curve shape approximated from Northrop Grumman QM-1 test data.
notes: Inert mass = 730 t gross minus 631 t propellant. Curve shape is approximate.

name: Space Shuttle SRB
source: NASA Space Shuttle News Reference Manual (1988), SRB section; thrust-curve shape approximated from the published RSRM trace.
notes: Curve shape is approximate; it includes the max-Q thrust bucket.

name: S-IC stage structure and tanks
source: NASA Saturn V Flight Manual SA-503; Apollo 11 (AS-506) Saturn V Launch Vehicle Flight Evaluation Report, MPR-SAT-FE-69-9.
notes: Dry mass excludes the five F-1 engines (listed separately).

name: S-IC/S-II interstage
source: NASA Saturn V Flight Manual SA-503.
notes: Really jettisoned ~30 s after S-II ignition; the sim drops it with the S-IC.

name: S-II stage structure and tanks
source: NASA Saturn V Flight Manual SA-503.
notes: Dry mass excludes the five J-2 engines.

name: S-II/S-IVB interstage
source: NASA Saturn V Flight Manual SA-503.

name: S-IVB stage structure and tanks
source: NASA Saturn V Flight Manual SA-503.
notes: Dry mass excludes the J-2. Propellant covers both the orbit burn and the trans-lunar injection burn.

name: Instrument Unit
source: NASA Saturn V Flight Manual SA-503.

name: Spacecraft-LM adapter
source: NASA Apollo 11 Press Kit (1969).

name: Apollo Lunar Module
source: NASA Apollo 11 Press Kit (1969).
notes: Fuelled mass. Rides inside the adapter.

name: Apollo Service Module
source: NASA Apollo 11 Press Kit (1969).
notes: Fuelled mass.

name: Apollo Command Module
source: NASA Apollo 11 Press Kit (1969).
notes: Heat-shield ratings are estimates, set so the safe lunar-return corridor is about −6° to −7.5°, close to Apollo's.

name: Launch escape tower
source: NASA Apollo 11 Press Kit (1969).

name: A1-39 core thrust section
source: Free-design estimate (Super Heavy class thrust structure).

name: A1-39 core tank (10 m)
source: Free-design rule: volume × methalox bulk density (832.6 kg/m³ at O/F 3.6) × 90% usable; dry mass 4.5% of propellant.

name: A1-39 interstage (10 m to 6 m)
source: Free-design estimate.

name: A1-39 core fin
source: Free-design estimate.

name: A1-39 landing leg
source: Free-design estimate (scaled from Falcon 9 legs).

name: A1-39 stage 2 engine skirt
source: Free-design estimate.

name: A1-39 stage 2 tank (6 m)
source: Free-design rule: volume × methalox bulk density (832.6 kg/m³ at O/F 3.6) × 90% usable; dry mass 5.5% of propellant.

name: Lunar module adapter panels
source: Free-design estimate, scaled from the Apollo spacecraft-LM adapter.

name: A1-39 service module
source: Free-design estimate, scaled from Apollo (includes ~16 t propellant and the methalox SM engine).

name: A1-39 command module
source: Free-design estimate, scaled from the Apollo command module.
notes: Heat-shield ratings are estimates, set so the safe lunar-return corridor is about −6° to −7.5°, close to Apollo's.

name: A1-39 escape tower
source: Free-design estimate, scaled from the Apollo launch escape system.

name: SpaceX Merlin 1D
source: SpaceX Falcon 9 user's guide and public statements (Full Thrust), compiled in Wikipedia 'SpaceX Merlin'.
notes: Block 5 figures; mass is a third-party estimate.

name: SpaceX Merlin Vacuum
source: SpaceX Falcon 9 user's guide (981 kN, 348 s). Sea-level figures derived from a 3.3 m nozzle exit and are not a real rating.

name: Falcon 9 first-stage tanks
source: SpaceX (411 t propellant, Block 5). Dry mass about 25.6 t including engines, legs and grid fins (third-party estimate); engines, legs and interstage listed separately.

name: Falcon 9 interstage
source: Third-party estimate (carbon composite, ~2 t).

name: Falcon 9 landing leg
source: Third-party estimate (four carbon/aluminium legs, ~2 t total). Touchdown limit is an assumption.

name: Falcon 9 second-stage tanks
source: SpaceX (107.5 t propellant). Dry mass about 4 t including the Merlin Vacuum (third-party estimate).

name: Falcon Heavy centre-core tanks
source: Falcon 9 tanks, strengthened to carry the side boosters' loads; extra mass is an estimate.

name: Falcon Heavy side booster (9 Merlins)
source: Falcon 9 first stage with a nose cone. Burn time from Falcon Heavy webcasts (side-booster cutoff near T+2:30).
notes: Liquid-fuelled, but modelled as a strap-on that burns at full thrust until empty: the real ones throttle a little and fly back to land.

name: Cargo Dragon (with cargo and trunk)
source: NASA CRS fact sheets: Dragon 1 about 4.2 t dry, up to 3.3 t of cargo, plus the trunk. Heat-shield ratings use the same basis as the Apollo capsule.
notes: PICA-X heat shield; real ratings are higher than this conservative figure.

name: Payload fairing (5.2 m)
source: SpaceX Falcon user's guide (5.2 m × 13.1 m); mass a third-party estimate.
notes: Drawn as a capsule shape; drops away once the air is thin.

name: Little satellite
source: Example small satellite (Sputnik 1 was 84 kg; small weather and science satellites are a few hundred kg).
notes: Rides inside the nose, so it is not drawn.

name: Heavy satellite
source: Example payload for a heavy-lift flight to low orbit.
notes: Rides inside the fairing, so it is not drawn.

name: Moon base module
source: Space Q design: a small habitat module, about the mass of an ISS node module's contents and structure scaled down.
notes: Rides on the cargo lander, so it is not drawn separately.

name: Space Q cargo lander
source: Space Q design: a one-way methane lander that brakes into Moon orbit and lands its cargo. Sized like the Apollo descent stage scaled up, with a methalox engine.
notes: Fuelled mass. No ascent stage: it stays on the Moon with the cargo.

name: Little planet probe
source: Mariner 2 (1962) weighed 203 kg; rounded up for a small modern flyby probe.
notes: Flyby only: no big engine. Rides inside the nose, so it is not drawn.

name: Armored probe
source: Space Q design: the little planet probe wrapped in thick metal plates to stop asteroid hits. Real probes don't need this: the belt is mostly empty.
notes: Rides inside the nose, so it is not drawn.

name: Mars orbiter
source: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (2005): 2,180 kg at launch with 1,149 kg of hydrazine; six 170 N main thrusters.
notes: Its own engine brakes it into orbit. Isp is an estimate for its hydrazine thrusters.

name: Sun-side probe
source: MESSENGER (2004): 1,107 kg at launch with about 600 kg of propellant and a 660 N bipropellant engine (Isp about 317 s).
notes: A sunshade keeps it cool so close to the Sun.

name: Ion probe
source: Dawn (2007): 1,218 kg at launch with 425 kg of xenon; NSTAR ion engines at about 3,100 s Isp and 91 mN thrust.
notes: Super fuel-saving, but its push is gentle (about the weight of a sheet of paper), so trips take years.

name: Space Q sample-return probe
source: Space Q design: a Dawn-style ion probe with over three times the xenon, three engines firing at once, a sample arm like OSIRIS-REx's, and a small heat-shielded capsule like Stardust's for the trip back down.
notes: The sample capsule drops into Earth's air on its own and parachutes down.

name: Space Q braking stage
source: Space Q design: a storable-propellant kick stage (like a Fregat or the Apollo service engine) that waits through the cruise and fires to brake at the far end.
notes: Fires first when braking, then drops off when empty; the probe's own engine does the rest.

name: Rover with only a parachute
source: Space Q test: a Perseverance-size rover in its heat shield and backshell, with the parachute but no landing rockets.
notes: Shows why Mars needs rockets as well: its air is too thin for a parachute alone.

name: Rover with sky crane
source: Mars 2020 / Perseverance: about 3,650 kg entering Mars (rover 1,025 kg, descent stage with about 400 kg of hydrazine, heat shield and backshell). Eight throttled hydrazine engines.
notes: Heat shield, then a supersonic parachute, then the sky crane lowers the rover on cables.

name: Space Q Mars lander
source: Space Q design: a 7 m heat shield, big parachutes and methane landing engines, carrying about 8 t of supplies for a future crew.
notes: One-way cargo lander for Mars.

name: Venus lander
source: Venera 13 (1982): about 760 kg lander inside a 2.4 m entry shell, part of a 4,400 kg spacecraft. It sent pictures for 127 minutes.
notes: A ball-shaped pressure hull, padded and pre-chilled before landing.

name: Space Q cool lander
source: Space Q design: a thicker hull, more insulation and a big block of ice-cold phase-change material to soak up heat. A guess at about five hours.
notes: Heavier, but lasts longer in Venus's 465 °C air.

name: RS-25 (Shuttle main engine, 104.5%)
source: NASA Space Shuttle News Reference; Aerojet Rocketdyne RS-25 data, compiled in Wikipedia 'RS-25' (scaled from 109% to 104.5%).

name: Shuttle external tank (super lightweight)
source: NASA (SLWT: 26.5 t empty, about 760 t loaded).

name: Space Shuttle orbiter
source: NASA: orbiter about 78 t empty including its three main engines (listed separately here), plus OMS/RCS propellant, crew and a 20 t payload.
notes: Rides on the side of the tank. It glides home like a plane, so there is no capsule re-entry for it in the sim.

name: RS-25 (SLS, 109%)
source: Aerojet Rocketdyne RS-25 data at 109% power, compiled in Wikipedia 'RS-25'.

name: RL10B-2
source: Aerojet Rocketdyne RL10B-2 data sheet. Sea-level figures derived from the nozzle exit and are not a real rating.

name: SLS core stage
source: NASA SLS reference guide (core stage about 85 t dry with engines, 987 t of propellant).

name: Launch vehicle stage adapter
source: NASA SLS reference guide (LVSA); mass a third-party estimate.

name: Interim cryogenic propulsion stage
source: ULA Delta IV 5 m upper stage, NASA ICPS fact sheet.

name: Orion stage adapter
source: NASA SLS reference guide; mass estimate.

name: Orion European Service Module
source: ESA ESM fact sheet (about 15.5 t with 8.6 t of propellant; AJ10 main engine).

name: Orion crew module
source: NASA Orion reference guide (crew module about 10.4 t; three 35 m mains). Heat-shield ratings use the same basis as Apollo.

name: Orion launch abort system
source: NASA Orion reference guide.

name: Super Heavy booster tanks
source: SpaceX public statements (about 3,400 t of propellant); dry mass about 200 t with engines is a third-party estimate.

name: Hot-staging ring
source: Third-party estimate.
notes: The real ship lights its engines before separating (hot staging); the sim separates first.

name: Super Heavy grid fin
source: Third-party estimate.

name: Tower catch pins
source: Assumption: the tower arms catch the booster if it arrives slowly enough.

name: Starship upper stage tanks
source: SpaceX public statements (about 1,500 t of propellant on the Block 2 ship); dry mass about 100 t with engines and heat shield is a third-party estimate.

name: Starship nose and payload bay
source: Third-party estimate.

name: Cargo (100 t)
source: SpaceX goal for Starship to low orbit.
notes: Inside the payload bay, so it is not drawn.
